# Handover: T-2 background job logging landed (2026-09-20)

Targeted autonomous session, `/story auto T-2`. One target, completed. Commit `3821fbb` on `main`.

## Completed

- **T-2: Add logging for background jobs** — `JobQueue.run()` emits `job started` / `job succeeded` / `job failed` through AppLogger, one logger per job bound to `QueuedJob.requestId`. Six tests in `src/jobs/JobQueue.test.ts`. Suite is 10/10.
- Cited **r-eftp2zdb6as643np** and **r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma** on T-2 (it cited neither, so neither was reaching the review stages).

## Decisions

- **`JobRunner` widened to `(job, log) => ...`.** r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma governs *anything* a job logs, not just the three lines JobQueue emits. Under the old one-arg signature a runner's path of least resistance is minting a fresh id, which violates the ruling while every queue-level test stays green. Handing the bound logger down is the `Router`/`RouteHandler` precedent and makes it structural. Backward compatible — a `(job) => ...` runner still assigns.
- **`enqueue()` rejects a blank request id.** A job without one cannot be logged under its own id, and both escapes are forbidden (fresh id by r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma, dropping lines by r-eftp2zdb6as643np). This is a contract check for direct non-HTTP callers — it is *not* reachable from the HTTP path, since `Router.dispatch` builds the logger first. The reachable hole is ISS-001.
- **`job.payload` is deliberately not logged.** It is caller-controlled `unknown` (literally `req.body` on the HTTP path) and `redact()` only catches secret-shaped values or secret-named keys, so a secret under a neutral key would reach the line. The tests assert a *closed* field set (`assert.deepEqual`), which is what pins this — an open key-presence check would let a later change add it back silently.
- **No `finally`, and the success log sits outside the `try`.** A `finally` would log a failed job as succeeded. Keeping `ran++` and the success log inside the `try` had the mirror bug: a throwing sink counted one job both ways (`{ran: 2, failed: 2}`) and logged a succeeded job as failed. Now only the runner is guarded; a broken sink propagates as the infrastructure error it is.
- **`src/http/handler.ts` deliberately untouched.** An earlier plan draft wired the injected sink into the default queue; dropped because `createApp` never exposes the queue and `JobQueue.run()` has zero callers, so nothing could observe it and it would be a signature change with no test in its own directory (RULES #3). Recorded as ISS-003.

## Rejected approach

Exposing the queue or a `drain()` from `createApp` to get an end-to-end HTTP→enqueue→run test. It is the stronger proof that the request id survives the whole chain, but it widens `createApp`'s public API to serve a caller that does not exist yet. Revisit when something actually drains the app-level queue — that is the moment to do it, and ISS-003 is where it is written down.

## Issues filed

- **ISS-001** (medium) — `handler.ts:31` mints the request id with `?? randomUUID()`, which does not catch `""`. A client sending an empty `x-request-id` header makes `Router.dispatch` throw and `app.handle` reject. Fix is to normalize at the boundary; does not conflict with r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma.
- **ISS-002** (low) — no `@types/node`, so `tsc --noEmit` fails on every file using a Node built-in and the project cannot actually be typechecked despite `strict: true`. A real type error did hide in that noise this session. The obvious fix (`npm i -D @types/node`) sits against RULES #2, so whether that rule covers devDependencies is an **owner call**.
- **ISS-003** (low) — `createApp`'s default `JobQueue` ignores the injected sink, so job lines and route lines would go to different destinations for whoever first drains the queue.

## Notes for next session

- Both review stages ran on the **agent** backend: the `review_plan` MCP tool (codex bridge) is not registered in this environment. Plan review took two rounds; code review approved in one with two minors, both fixed and verified by mutation before the report.
- Mutation testing is what caught the weakest test: deleting the `await` in `run()` left all 9 tests green until an async-rejecting-runner test was added. Worth repeating on anything that awaits.
- `storybloq` MCP reports a version skew (server v1.15.9 vs v0.0.1 installed); a Claude Code restart would clear it.

## Continuation

- **ISS-001** is the highest-value follow-up: a real request-path crash, small fix, and it is the half of the blank-id story T-2 could not close.
- **ISS-002** needs an owner decision before anyone can act on it.

## Carried forward

- T-3 — move AppLogger into `packages/logging` once a second service needs it. Untouched.

content.impact: src/http/handler.ts:31 mints the request id with `req.headers["x-request-id"] ?? randomUUID()`. `??` only falls back on null/undefined, so a client sending an empty or whitespace-only `x-request-id` yields a blank id. Router.dispatch then calls AppLogger.withRequestId at src/http/router.ts:37, which throws "AppLogger requires a non-empty request id" before any route body runs, so app.handle rejects and the request 500s/crashes instead of being served under a fresh id. Fix: normalize at the boundary, e.g. `const raw = req.headers["x-request-id"]; const requestId = raw !== undefined && raw.trim() !== "" ? raw : randomUUID()`. This does not conflict with r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma, which constrains a job inheriting the enqueuing request's id, not how handler.ts mints an id for a request that supplied none. Found during T-2 plan review; pre-existing and out of scope for T-2, which touches src/jobs/.
content.title: Blank x-request-id header produces an unhandled rejection from app.handle

content.impact: `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` reports TS2307 "Cannot find module 'node:test' / 'node:assert/strict' / 'node:crypto'" and TS2580 "Cannot find name 'process'" on pristine HEAD, across src/http/handler.ts, src/http/router.test.ts, src/platform/logging/AppLogger.ts and AppLogger.test.ts. The cause is that no @types/node is installed (there is no node_modules and package.json declares no devDependencies). Consequence: tsconfig.json sets `strict: true` and `noEmit: true`, but nothing can actually typecheck the project, and `npm test` is `node --test`, which strips types without checking them. A genuine type error therefore reaches main unnoticed - one did surface during T-2 (TS18048 in a new test, masked among the resolution noise). Resolving this is an owner call, because the obvious fix (`npm i --save-dev @types/node`) sits against RULES.md #2 "Keep the code dependency-free: Node built-ins only" - whether that rule is about runtime dependencies only, or about devDependencies too, is not settled anywhere in the repo. Found during T-2 implementation verification; pre-existing and out of scope for T-2.
content.title: Project cannot be typechecked: no @types/node, so tsc --noEmit fails on every file using a Node built-in

content.impact: src/http/handler.ts:17 is `createApp(queue: JobQueue = new JobQueue(), sink?: Sink)`. The default queue is constructed before `sink` is in play, so `createApp(undefined, sink)` yields route lines on the injected sink and job lines on AppLogger's default stdout sink. Harmless today and deliberately left alone by T-2: `createApp` never exposes the queue and `JobQueue.run()` has zero callers in src, so nothing drains the app-level queue and no test can observe the split. It becomes a real trap for whoever first drains it - job logging would silently bypass a test's sink, and a test asserting on job lines would see none. Fix when that caller appears: `createApp(queue?: JobQueue, sink?: Sink)` with `const jobs = queue ?? new JobQueue(sink)`, together with whatever makes the queue reachable (returning it, or a `drain(runner)` from createApp), so the change is observable in a test under src/http/ per RULES.md #3. Raised in T-2 code review; T-2 deliberately scoped itself to src/jobs/.
content.title: createApp's default JobQueue ignores the injected sink, so job lines and route lines go to different destinations

content.content: Before reporting a review round as clean, break the thing the test claims to pin and confirm the suite goes red. If nothing fails, the test proves nothing, whatever it asserts. Most valuable on awaits, ordering, and counts — where the right result appears for the wrong reason.
content.context: T-2 (background job logging). JobQueue.test.ts had five tests and all passed, but every runner was synchronous, so `await runner(job, log)` was never exercised — deleting the `await` left all 9 tests green. Under that implementation an async runner that rejects is counted in `ran` and logged as "job succeeded" while the rejection escapes unhandled, which is exactly the failure the ticket existed to make visible. Caught by code review mutating the implementation, not by reading the tests. The same technique confirmed the fix (dropping the await now fails exactly one test) and confirmed a second finding: a throwing sink had been counting one job both ways as {ran: 2, failed: 2}.
content.title: Mutate the implementation to prove a test actually tests it

content.content: At PLAN, list the project's current rulings and cite the ones that bind the item, even when it cites none. Rulings reach reviewers by citation only — an uncited ruling is invisible to every review stage, so the gate that should catch a violation never sees the rule.
content.context: T-2 recorded no citesRulings. Two current rulings governed every line it added (r-eftp2zdb6as643np on redaction and request ids, r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma on background work carrying the enqueuing request id). Citing them at PLAN put both into the plan-review and code-review context packets, and r-p19bbvh0jhj8xgma's "anything it logs" wording is what drove widening JobRunner to hand the runner its bound logger — a design decision that would not have been made if the ruling had stayed uncited. Note one ruling in this project (r-rvcf99q7dwhzzpav) is superseded: cite the current id, not the one an older handover mentions.
content.title: Cite the rulings that bind an item before planning it
